## What this document is {.unnumbered}

This is two things at once. It is a tutorial for **ggcarto**, an R package that
adds cartographic colour scales to ggplot2. And it is a short course in the
cartography those scales implement: *why* maps class their data into intervals,
*why* the choice of interval method changes what a map says, *how many* classes
to use and how to defend the number, *why* map colour follows rules that
ordinary charts get away with ignoring, and *why* two variables on one map need
a very particular kind of legend.

Every idea is shown on a real map — the 217 counties of the US Northeast, from
Pennsylvania to Maine — and every claim about how people read maps is tied to
the research that established it. You need to know a little R and a little
ggplot2. You do not need to know anything about cartography.

The package is organised around one sequence, and so is this document:

> **inspect → choose → classify → map → diagnose**

Look at the distribution before you class it. Choose the number of classes
with the trade-offs in front of you. Classify with a method you can name and
defend. Draw the map. Then read the decisions back off the finished map and
check they are the ones you meant to make.

## Setup

### Install

ggcarto lives on GitHub. It needs ggplot2 and classInt; sf draws the polygons,
and the other packages below are used for layout and tables.

```{r}
#| label: install
#| eval: false
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("jcapellan/ggcarto")
install.packages(c("sf", "dplyr", "patchwork", "RColorBrewer", "viridisLite",
                   "colorspace"))
```

```{r}
#| label: libraries
library(ggcarto)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)
theme_set(theme_ggcarto(base_size = 12, legend = "right"))
```

### The data: the counties of the Northeast

ggcarto ships `northeast_counties`: an sf object with the 217 counties of the
Census Bureau's Northeast region and a handful of variables from the American
Community Survey 2015–2019 [@acs2019], compiled from the usdata package
[@usdata]. It is already projected (an Albers equal-area conic centred on the
region), so `geom_sf()` draws it correctly with no further work.

```{r}
#| label: data
data(northeast_counties)
cty <- northeast_counties
cty
```

The variables were chosen because they misbehave in different, instructive
ways:

| Variable | What it is | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| `unemployment` | unemployment rate, % | nearly symmetric — the easy case |
| `median_income` | median household income, $ | moderately right-skewed |
| `pop` | population | a heavy right tail: New York City's boroughs against rural Maine |
| `pct_bachelors` | adults with a bachelor's degree, % | wide, lumpy: metro against rural |
| `pct_poverty` | people below the poverty line, % | 49 counties missing |

```{r}
#| label: shapes
#| fig-height: 5
cty |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(unemployment, median_income, pop, pct_bachelors, pct_poverty) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free", ncol = 5) +
  theme_minimal(10) +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank())
```

::: {.callout-note}
## sf is not required by ggcarto
Every scale in this document works identically with `geom_polygon()`,
`geom_tile()` or `geom_point()`. Nothing in ggcarto depends on the geometry
layer; sf is used here because it is what most people map with.
:::

`theme_ggcarto()` is the package's map theme -- warm paper, a navy title,
grey annotation, no axes, legend under the map -- and it is set as the
default above. One helper, so that each map is one line and side-by-side
maps get a compact legend underneath:

```{r}
#| label: helper
ne_map <- function(var = "unemployment", data = cty, title = NULL) {
  ggplot(data) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data[[var]]), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
    labs(title = title, fill = NULL) +
    theme(legend.key.height = unit(1.1, "lines"),
          plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
}

bottom_legend <- function(rows = 2) {
  list(theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
             legend.key.size = unit(0.9, "lines")),
       guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = rows, byrow = TRUE, reverse = TRUE)))
}
```

## The problem, in one picture

Here is county unemployment drawn the way ggplot2 draws it if you do nothing:

```{r}
#| label: default
#| fig-height: 5
ne_map(title = "Unemployment rate: ggplot2 defaults")
```

It is not wrong. It is just hard to *use*. Try to answer "which counties are
above 6%?" from that legend. The ramp is smooth, so any two nearby counties
look the same; the darkest blue is the *lowest* value, which is backwards from
what most readers expect; and there is no way to state what a colour *means*.

Now the same data with five classes, a palette made for maps, and labels that
read like sentences:

```{r}
#| label: fixed-classes
#| fig-height: 5
ne_map(title = "Unemployment rate: five classes") +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlOrRd", style = "fisher", n = 5,
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%",
                                          digits = 1, open = TRUE),
                       na.value = "grey85")
```

Everything in this document is about the decisions hiding inside that second
call: how many classes, where the breaks go, which palette, how the legend is
worded, what happens to a county with no data. None of these are cosmetic.
Each one changes what a reader will conclude.

## Why maps are not charts

### Colour is a weak channel

In a scatterplot, *position* carries the number. Our visual system judges
position along a common scale very accurately: in Cleveland and McGill's
experiments, position was the most accurately decoded of all the "elementary
perceptual tasks", and colour saturation and shading were the least
[@cleveland1984]. Bertin made the same point from the design side: of the visual
variables available to a map, only *size* and *value* (lightness) are reliably
read as ordered quantities, and lightness supports only a handful of
distinguishable steps [@bertin1983].

On a choropleth map, colour is the *only* channel carrying the number. Position
is spent on geography. So the map is asking the reader to do the one perceptual
task they are worst at, and it should ask as little as possible.

### Classing makes the map answerable

That is the argument for classing. A continuous ramp promises precision — every
county its own shade — that the reader cannot extract. Five or six classes turn
the map into a set of yes/no questions the eye *can* answer ("is this county in
the darkest class?"), and turn the legend into something a reader can hold in
memory: "dark red means 6% or more".

Cartography textbooks converge on five to seven classes for a single-hue
scheme [@slocum2009; @dent2009; @brewer2016]. Fewer than three shows no
pattern; more than seven and readers can no longer match a colour on the map
back to the legend. With a diverging scheme, use an odd number so there is a
neutral middle class.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When *not* to class
Continuous ramps are fine when colour is a secondary channel (a heatmap where
position already encodes the cells, a scatterplot coloured by a third
variable), when the audience is reading *shape* rather than *values* (a raster
of elevation), or when the map is interactive and the value appears on hover.
ggcarto's `scale_fill_cont()` is there for those cases.
:::

### Why the breaks matter so much

Classing throws information away, and where the breaks fall decides which
information survives. Here are four maps of the same variable with the same
number of classes and the same palette. Only the classification method differs.

```{r}
#| label: four-methods
#| fig-height: 8
methods <- c("equal", "quantile", "fisher", "sd")
maps4 <- lapply(methods, function(st) {
  ne_map("pct_bachelors", title = paste0('style = "', st, '"')) +
    scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", style = st, n = 5,
                         labels = label_map(style = "interval", digits = 0,
                                            open = TRUE, suffix = "%")) +
    bottom_legend()
})
wrap_plots(maps4, ncol = 2)
```

Four honest maps, four different stories. Equal intervals says most of the
Northeast is in the middle and only a ring of suburban counties stands out.
Quantiles say the Boston–New York–Philadelphia corridor is one thing and
everything else is another. Fisher's natural breaks land in between. Standard
deviations centre the story on "above or below the regional average".

So the classification is an *argument*, not a setting, and you should be able
to say which question your map answers [@monmonier2018]:

| The question the map answers | Method that fits |
|---|---|
| Where are the high (or low) values? | natural breaks (`fisher`, `jenks`) |
| How is this spread across the region? Which counties are in the top fifth? | `quantile` |
| Which counties are above the average, and by how much? | `sd` |
| Is this above the policy threshold? | fixed breaks you choose |
| How does this year compare with last year? | the *same* fixed breaks both years |
| Where are the extreme cases in a heavy-tailed variable? | `headtails`, `log` |

## Inspect: see the distribution and the breaks

### What a break is

A class interval method takes a numeric variable and returns `n + 1` cut points
that split it into `n` classes. In ggcarto that is one function:

```{r}
#| label: compute-breaks
compute_breaks(cty$unemployment, style = "quantile", n = 5)
compute_breaks(cty$unemployment, style = "fisher",   n = 5)
compute_breaks(cty$unemployment, style = "equal",    n = 5)
```

Every style is also available as a *factory* — `breaks_quantile(5)` returns a
function that computes those breaks from whatever data it is given — so a style
can be handed to a scale and evaluated later, when the scale finally sees the
data:

```{r}
#| label: factories
f <- breaks_jenks(6)
f
f(cty$unemployment)
```

`map_styles_info()` is the in-package cheat sheet:

```{r}
#| label: styles-info
knitr::kable(map_styles_info())
```

### Seeing where the breaks fall

The best way to understand a method is to draw its breaks on the histogram of
the variable. `plot_breaks()` does that for one method and `compare_breaks()`
for several, over the same histogram, with each class shaded and annotated
with its count:

```{r}
#| label: compare-breaks-unemp
#| fig-height: 8
compare_breaks(cty$unemployment,
               c("equal", "pretty", "quantile", "fisher", "sd", "headtails"),
               n = 5)
```

Read the panels top to bottom.

**Equal interval** (`equal`) slices the *range* into equal widths. It is honest
about magnitude — one step in colour is one step in value — and it is what a
reader assumes a legend means unless told otherwise. On a nearly symmetric
variable like this one it works; on a skewed one it does not, as the
population section shows. `pretty` is the same idea with the cut points rounded
to numbers people can read (4, 6, 8 ...), which is why it is ggplot2's own
default for binned scales.

**Quantile** (`quantile`) puts equal *counts* in each class. Every class is
populated, the map is visually balanced, and the legend can be read as "top
fifth of counties". The cost is that class widths become unequal and the map
hides that. In Brewer and Pickle's map-reading experiment with 56 subjects and
nine series of US mortality maps, quantiles nonetheless produced the most
accurate answers to general map-reading questions, and "the advantages of
careful optimization procedures in choropleth classification seem to offer no
benefit over the simpler quantile method" [@brewer2002].

**Natural breaks** (`fisher`, `jenks`, and the clustering variants `kmeans`,
`hclust`, `bclust`) look for gaps in the data. Formally they choose breaks that
minimise the variance *within* classes and maximise it *between* them
[@jenks1967; @jenks1971]. `fisher` is Walter Fisher's exact dynamic-programming
solution to that problem [@fisher1958]; `jenks` is George Jenks's iterative
approximation of it, the one built into GIS software. They give near-identical
results; `fisher` is faster and is the one to use. Natural breaks follow the
data's own structure, which is why they are the sensible default for a single
map. The two costs are that the cut points look arbitrary (4.3%, 5.1%) and are
specific to *this* dataset, so two maps classed by natural breaks are not
comparable [@coulson1987; @evans1977].

**Standard deviation** (`sd`) puts the breaks at the mean and at ±1, ±2 ... SD
from it. Use it when the question is "above or below average, and by how
much", and pair it with a diverging palette so the mean is the neutral colour.
It only makes sense for roughly symmetric data — which unemployment is.

**Head/tail breaks** (`headtails`) is for heavy-tailed variables — populations,
incomes, anything where a few areas dwarf the rest [@jiang2013]. It splits at
the mean, keeps the values above the mean (the "head"), splits that at *its*
mean, and repeats until the head is no longer a minority. It chooses its own
class count, and on a symmetric variable it stops early. That is the method
telling you it is the wrong tool for these data; it comes into its own on
population, below.

Three more, for completeness: `box` uses the quartiles and the 1.5·IQR
fences from a boxplot, so outliers get their own classes; `dpih` uses
kernel-density bandwidth selection to choose histogram bins [@wand1997];
`maximum` splits at the widest empty gaps in the sorted values. All of these
except `equal`, `pretty`, `quantile`, `sd`, `log`, `geometric` and `unique` are
computed by the **classInt** package [@classint], which is the reference
implementation in R.

::: {.callout-note}
## Exact, and the same every time
classInt takes a shortcut on large vectors: above 3,000 values it computes
`fisher` and `jenks` on a random 10% sample, and the sample is drawn from the
session's random number generator, so a map of the 3,100 US counties could
class differently every time it was drawn. ggcarto turns that off. Fisher is
computed exactly at any size (about 0.3 s for 10,000 values), and every style
with a random component (`kmeans`, `bclust`) is seeded. `?compute_breaks`
documents the details and the `large_n` argument that restores the shortcut,
reproducibly, if you need it.
:::

### Heavy tails: population

County population is the textbook heavy-tailed variable — the median county in
the region has 100,000 people and Kings County (Brooklyn) has 2.6 million.
Watch equal intervals and quantiles fail in opposite ways, and the
transform-aware styles cope:

```{r}
#| label: compare-breaks-pop
#| fig-height: 8
compare_breaks(cty$pop, c("equal", "quantile", "fisher", "headtails", "log", "geometric"),
               n = 5, log_x = TRUE)
```

On a log axis the equal-interval breaks all pile up at the right — four of the
five classes hold a handful of counties between them. `log` puts breaks at 1,
2, 5 per decade; `geometric` uses a constant ratio between breaks; `headtails`
stops when the tail stops. On the map:

```{r}
#| label: pop-maps
#| fig-height: 4.6
p1 <- ne_map("pop", title = 'style = "equal" (useless)') +
  scale_fill_intervals("viridis::mako", style = "equal", n = 5, reverse = TRUE,
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", big.mark = ",")) +
  bottom_legend(3)
p2 <- ne_map("pop", title = 'style = "log"') +
  scale_fill_intervals("viridis::mako", style = "log", n = 6, reverse = TRUE,
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", big.mark = ",")) +
  bottom_legend(3)
p1 | p2
```

## Choose: how many classes?

There is no optimal number of classes. There is a trade-off between four
things: how faithfully the classes reproduce the distribution (*fit*), whether
every class has enough counties in it to be worth a colour (*balance*),
whether the break values are far enough apart to mean anything (*separation*),
and how many ordered colours a reader can tell apart (*perception*).
`class_guide()` computes all four for every candidate count and applies a
small set of stated rules — different rules for different families of method —
to make a suggestion. It says *suggested*, not *optimal*, on purpose.

```{r}
#| label: class-guide
g <- class_guide(cty$pct_bachelors, style = "fisher")
g
```

The *fit* column is the goodness of variance fit, $1 - SSW/SST$, the quantity
Jenks and Caspall proposed for exactly this purpose [@jenks1971]: 0 for one
class, 1 when every class is constant. The rules for a natural-breaks method
are: a candidate needs every class populated; take the smallest count whose
fit is at least 0.80 and whose gain to the next count is under 0.05 (where the
curve flattens); step down if that leaves a class with under 2% of the
counties and little fit is lost; never go past seven when a seven-or-fewer
solution is close. `?class_guide` states them all, and `summary()` and
`plot()` show the numbers behind them.

```{r}
#| label: class-guide-plot
#| fig-height: 5
plot(g)
```

```{r}
#| label: class-guide-balance
#| fig-height: 4
plot(g, type = "balance")
```

The rules are method-specific because the methods are. For `quantile` the
classes are balanced by construction, so fit is beside the point; the guide
instead checks whether adding classes forces breaks so close together that the
legend draws distinctions the data cannot support. For `equal` it counts the
classes the skew has emptied. For `headtails` it reports the count the method
chose and why, because `n` is not part of that method. For `fixed` it declines
to recommend anything: the thresholds are yours.

```{r}
#| label: class-guide-others
class_guide(cty$pop, style = "equal")
class_guide(cty$pop, style = "headtails")
```

::: {.callout-important}
## A suggestion, not an answer
`class_guide()` encodes the conventional trade-offs and shows its working. It
does not know what your map is *for*. If the policy threshold is 10%, use a
break at 10%. If the map will sit next to last year's, use last year's breaks.
The guide is where to start the argument, not where to end it.
:::

## Classify: the numbers behind the legend

The guide suggested four classes for the share of graduates and offered five
as a defensible alternative. For a map whose point is the gradient from rural
to metropolitan counties, the extra class is worth the extra legend line, so
the rest of this section uses five — which is the kind of judgement the guide
leaves to you. Once you have a method and a count, `class_summary()` gives the
classes as a table: the bounds, the label the legend will carry, and how many
counties fall in each. It uses the same break engine as the scales, so what
it reports is what the map will draw.

```{r}
#| label: class-summary
class_summary(cty$pct_bachelors, "fisher", 5)
```

And `plot_breaks()` puts those classes on the histogram:

```{r}
#| label: plot-breaks
#| fig-height: 3.4
plot_breaks(cty$pct_bachelors, "fisher", 5)
```

### Where does a value *on* the break go?

A value of exactly 30 with a break at 30 has to go somewhere. ggplot2's binned
scales put it in the class *below* — the classes are `(a, b]` — and so does
ggcarto by default. classInt and tmap default to the other convention,
`[a, b)`. It rarely matters for continuous rates; it matters a great deal for
integer data and for policy thresholds, where "10 and above" should mean what
it says. The `closure` argument makes the choice explicit, and `class_summary()`
shows the consequence:

```{r}
#| label: closure
x <- c(1, 5, 10, 10, 10, 15, 20)
class_summary(x, breaks = c(0, 10, 20), closure = "right")$n   # 10 goes below
class_summary(x, breaks = c(0, 10, 20), closure = "left")$n    # 10 goes above
```

For counts — 0, 1, 2, 3 ... — `as_count = TRUE` goes further: breaks are
rounded to whole numbers, classes are left-closed, and the labels read the way
a count legend should, "0 to 4", "5 to 9", never "0 to 5", "5 to 10":

```{r}
#| label: as-count
set.seed(1)
k <- rpois(300, 3)
class_summary(k, "quantile", 4, as_count = TRUE)
```

### Fixed breaks and comparability

When a map will be compared with another map — this year against last year,
one state against another, one outcome against a related outcome — the breaks
should be the *same* on both. Brewer and Pickle found that matched legends
across a series increased map-comparison accuracy by roughly 28%
[@brewer2002]. The same applies when the breaks carry meaning outside the data
(a poverty line, a regulatory threshold, a round number the reader will
remember).

Both cases are `breaks =`:

```{r}
#| label: fixed-breaks
#| fig-height: 5
ne_map(title = "Unemployment rate: round-number breaks") +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlOrRd", breaks = c(0, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10),
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%",
                                          open = TRUE),
                       na.value = "grey85")
```

A working rule that survives most projects: run `class_guide()` and
`class_summary()` with `fisher` to see where the data's own gaps are, then
round those cut points to numbers a reader can repeat out loud, and use the
rounded set as fixed breaks. You get natural breaks' fit and a legend that
makes sense.

### The trap in plain ggplot2, and why ggcarto exists

ggplot2 has a binned scale, `scale_fill_binned()`, and it accepts a `breaks`
function. So you would expect this to give quantile classes:

```{r}
#| label: trap
p <- ggplot(cty, aes(pct_bachelors, median_income, colour = unemployment)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_binned(breaks = breaks_quantile(5))
b <- ggplot_build(p)
b$plot$scales$get_scales("colour")$get_breaks()
compute_breaks(cty$unemployment, "quantile", 5)
```

It does not. ggplot2 calls a binned scale's `breaks` function with the scale
*limits* — two numbers, the minimum and maximum — not with the data. Given two
numbers, every data-driven algorithm collapses to equal intervals, and nothing
warns you. The same trap catches a function passed as `limits`: it, too, sees
only the two endpoints, so a quantile-based trim would trim the wrong thing.
ggcarto's scales are built on small ggplot2 subclasses that keep the trained
values and hand the break and limit functions the real distribution. That one
fix is the reason the package exists; the rest is ergonomics around it.

## Map: the map-shaped details

### Outliers: squish, don't drop

ggplot2's continuous scales, when given `limits`, turn any value outside them
into `NA` and draw it in the missing-value colour. On a map that is the wrong
message: a county with an extreme value is not a county with no data. The
cartographic convention is to *clamp* — outliers get the colour of the end
class and the legend says "$110,000 and above". ggcarto's scales default to
`oob = "squish"` for this reason, and `trim_limits()` gives you a principled
way to choose limits that leave the outliers out of the ramp without dropping
them from the map:

```{r}
#| label: squish
#| fig-height: 4.2
p1 <- ne_map("median_income", title = "limits = full range") +
  scale_fill_cont("viridis::inferno", reverse = TRUE,
                  labels = label_map(prefix = "$", scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k"))
p2 <- ne_map("median_income", title = "limits = trim_limits(0.02, 0.98), oob = squish") +
  scale_fill_cont("viridis::inferno", reverse = TRUE,
                  limits = trim_limits(0.02, 0.98),
                  labels = label_map(prefix = "$", scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k"))
(p1 | p2) & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The left map spends the top of its ramp on the four suburban counties above
$100,000, so the other 213 are squeezed into the lower colours. The right map
gives the ramp to the bulk of the data and clamps the extremes.

### Diverging data: anchor the midpoint

A diverging palette has two hues meeting at a neutral colour. It is the right
choice only when the data have a *meaningful middle* — zero change, the
regional average, 50% of the vote — and the neutral colour must sit exactly on
that value [@brewer1994]. Two things go wrong otherwise: the palette's midpoint
drifts to the middle of the data range, and unequal ranges either side make one
hue look more intense than the other for the same distance from the middle.

`midpoint =` fixes the first; `symmetric_limits()` fixes the second. With
classed data, `midpoint` also nudges a class break to sit exactly on it, so the
neutral colour is a class boundary rather than the middle of a class.

```{r}
#| label: diverging
#| fig-height: 4.2
regional <- weighted.mean(cty$unemployment, cty$pop)
p1 <- ne_map(title = "Unemployment: no anchor") +
  scale_fill_cont("brewer::RdBu", reverse = TRUE)
p2 <- ne_map(title = sprintf("midpoint = regional rate (%.1f%%), symmetric limits", regional)) +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::RdBu", reverse = TRUE, n = 6,
                       midpoint = regional, limits = symmetric_limits(regional),
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%",
                                          digits = 1)) +
  bottom_legend()
(p1 | p2) & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

On the left, the neutral colour lands at about 5.6% — the middle of the data
range — so a county with the regional rate reads as "better than average". On
the right, white is the regional rate and the reds and blues are equal
distances from it.

### Missing data gets its own key

An area with no data should be a neutral colour that cannot be mistaken for a
low value, and the legend should say so [@brewer2016]. `na.value` sets the
colour. For categorical and ordinal scales ggplot2 draws the key itself and
`na.label` names it. Its binned and continuous legends have no slot for an NA
key, so for interval and continuous scales add `na_key()` to the plot; it
draws a filled square under the main legend and nothing on the map. Poverty is
missing for 49 of the 217 counties, which is what a real map looks like:

```{r}
#| label: missing
#| fig-height: 5
ne_map("pct_poverty", title = "Poverty rate: the missing counties have a legend entry") +
  scale_fill_intervals("hcl::Batlow", style = "quantile", n = 5, na.value = "grey85",
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", digits = 1, suffix = "%")) +
  na_key("No data (49 counties)", fill = "grey85")
```

### Legend labels that read like a legend

`label_map()` returns a labelling function. `style = "interval"` turns `n + 1`
break points into `n` range labels; `open = TRUE` writes the first and last as
"Under x" and "x and above" rather than showing the data extremes; `prefix`,
`suffix`, `big.mark` and `digits` do what they say. It works in any ggplot2
scale, not only ggcarto's.

```{r}
#| label: labels
label_map(suffix = "%", digits = 0)(c(2.5, 7.5, 12.5))
label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%", digits = 0)(c(0, 5, 10, 31))
label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%", digits = 0, open = TRUE)(c(0, 5, 10, 31))
label_map(prefix = "$", big.mark = ",", scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k")(c(12500, 48000))
```

Two conventions worth following. Round: nobody needs 12.93% in a legend
[@brewer2016]. And when the data extremes are not meaningful numbers, open the
end classes; "Under 5%" is a fact about the world, "1.2% to 5%" is a fact about
the dataset.

## Colour

### Three kinds of palette

Brewer's colour-use guidelines, the basis of ColorBrewer, sort palettes by the
kind of data they encode [@brewer1994; @harrower2003]:

* **Sequential** — one hue, light to dark, for ordered data with a low and a
  high. The lightness ramp does the work; hue is decoration.
* **Diverging** — two hues meeting at a neutral, for ordered data with a
  meaningful middle. (See the unemployment map above.)
* **Qualitative** — distinct hues at similar lightness, for categories with
  no order. Never for a number.

Ordered categories ("low / medium / high", or classes from an interval scale)
take a *sequential* palette, not a qualitative one. A rainbow is not a
sequential palette: its lightness goes up and down, so it creates visual
boundaries where the data have none and hides real ones, and it is unreadable
for the roughly 8% of men with red-green colour-vision deficiency
[@borland2007; @crameri2020].

```{r}
#| label: palette-kinds
#| fig-height: 2.6
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
show_palette("brewer::YlGnBu", 7)
show_palette("brewer::RdBu", 7)
show_palette("brewer::Set2", 7)
par(op)
```

### Checking a palette

Palettes fail in predictable ways: the palest class vanishes against a white
page; two adjacent classes are too close to separate on small polygons; a
red–green scheme collapses for a colour-blind reader; a "diverging" palette has
no neutral centre. `check_palette()` measures those things — CIELAB lightness
and colour difference, contrast against the background, and colour-vision
simulation via the colorspace package [@zeileis2020] — and says what each one
would do to the map:

```{r}
#| label: check-palette
check_palette("brewer::YlGnBu", 5)
check_palette("brewer::RdYlGn", 7)
```

`plot_palette()` shows the classes as a colour-blind reader would see them.
The thing to look for is a boundary between two classes that disappears in one
of the rows:

```{r}
#| label: plot-palette
#| fig-height: 3.6
plot_palette("brewer::RdYlGn", 7)
```

### Where good palettes come from

Nobody needs to design a palette from scratch. Several R packages carry
palettes that have been designed and tested, and they differ in what they are
for:

| Source | Prefix in ggcarto | Roughly how many | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| grDevices `hcl.colors()` | `hcl::` | 115 | Palettes built in perceptual HCL space, shipped with R itself; no dependency [@zeileis2020] |
| RColorBrewer | `brewer::` | 35 | Cynthia Brewer's ColorBrewer schemes, designed for maps, tested for colour-blind safety and print [@harrower2003; @rcolorbrewer] |
| viridisLite | `viridis::` | 8 | viridis, magma, plasma, inferno, cividis, mako, rocket, turbo: perceptually uniform, colour-blind safe [@smith2015; @viridislite] |
| cols4all | `c4a::` | ~700 | The palette library behind tmap, each scored for colour-blind friendliness and contrast [@cols4all] |
| paletteer | any `package::name` | ~2,500 | An index of palettes from dozens of other packages (scico, rcartocolor, MetBrewer, wesanderson ...) [@paletteer] |

ggcarto does not carry palettes of its own. `as_palette()` resolves any of the
above through one `"source::name"` syntax and returns a function of `n`:

```{r}
#| label: as-palette
as_palette("brewer::YlGnBu")(5)
as_palette("hcl::Zissou 1", reverse = TRUE)(5)
as_palette(c("#f7fbff", "#08306b"))(5)      # your own colours, interpolated
palette_sources()                            # which sources are installed
```

`map_palettes()` searches them:

```{r}
#| label: map-palettes
map_palettes("div", source = "brewer")
head(map_palettes(pattern = "blue"))
```

### Three palette tricks

**Trim the washed-out end.** The lightest colour of most sequential ramps is
nearly white and vanishes against a white page or a white county border.
`range = c(0.15, 1)` drops it — `check_palette()` will tell you when you need
to.

**Reverse when the ramp runs the wrong way.** Dark should mean *more* of
whatever the map is about. Several viridis palettes are light-at-the-top;
`reverse = TRUE`.

**Even or by value.** With classed data, `interpolate = "even"` (the default)
gives each class an evenly spaced colour from the ramp — what GIS software and
tmap do, and what makes classes distinguishable. `interpolate = "value"` places
each class's colour at its position along the data range, so a wide class sits
further along the ramp; it is more faithful to magnitude and less legible.

```{r}
#| label: palette-tricks
#| fig-height: 4.2
p1 <- ne_map("median_income", title = 'range = c(0, 1): first class is white') +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::Blues", style = "fisher", n = 5,
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                          scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k", digits = 0)) +
  bottom_legend()
p2 <- ne_map("median_income", title = 'range = c(0.2, 1)') +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::Blues", style = "fisher", n = 5, range = c(0.2, 1),
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                          scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k", digits = 0)) +
  bottom_legend()
p1 | p2
```

## Diagnose: read the decisions back off the map

A finished map shows colours. It does not show that the top class holds six
counties, that 4% of the values were squished into the end classes, that the
neutral colour sits at a midpoint outside the data, or that the missing-data
grey is a near match for class 2. `diagnose_map()` takes the finished ggplot,
finds the ggcarto scale and the variable behind it, and reports all of that —
with warnings phrased as what a reader would get wrong, not as faults:

```{r}
#| label: diagnose
final <- ne_map("median_income", title = "Median household income") +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", style = "fisher", n = 5,
                       range = c(0.15, 1), na.value = "grey85",
                       limits = trim_limits(0.02, 0.98),
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                          big.mark = ",", digits = 0, open = TRUE))
diagnose_map(final)
```

```{r}
#| label: final-map
#| fig-height: 5
final
```

The same diagnosis is available before you build anything, from a scale and a
vector: `diagnose_scale(scale_fill_intervals(...), cty$median_income)`. Here is
what it says about a map that gets three things wrong at once — a diverging
palette with no midpoint, too many classes, and a missing-data colour that
looks like a class:

```{r}
#| label: diagnose-bad
diagnose_scale(scale_fill_intervals("brewer::RdBu", "quantile", n = 8,
                                    na.value = "#d1e5f0"),
               cty$pct_poverty)$warnings
```

## One engine, five mappings

Everything so far used `scale_fill_intervals()`. It is one of five ways to
read a variable, and all five come from the same function, `scale_map()`;
`type` is the only thing that changes. This is the idea ggcarto borrows from
tmap [@tennekes2018]: *how a variable is mapped* is a choice you should be able
to change with one word, without rewriting the rest of the call.

| `type` | What it does | Shorthand |
|---|---|---|
| `"continuous"` | smooth ramp | `scale_fill_cont()` |
| `"intervals"` | classed into `n` bins by `style` | `scale_fill_intervals()` |
| `"categorical"` | unordered categories, qualitative palette | `scale_fill_cat()` |
| `"ordinal"` | ordered categories, sequential palette | `scale_fill_ord()` |
| `"rank"` | colour by position in the distribution | `scale_fill_rank()` |

`palette`, `limits`, `oob`, `reverse`, `range`, `na.value`, `labels`
and `name` mean the same thing in all five.

```{r}
#| label: five-types
#| fig-height: 10
cty$income_ord <- cut(cty$median_income, c(0, 50000, 65000, 85000, Inf),
                      labels = c("Under $50k", "$50k to $65k", "$65k to $85k", "$85k and above"))
maps5 <- list(
  ne_map("median_income", title = "continuous") +
    scale_fill_map("hcl::Batlow", type = "continuous",
                   labels = label_map(prefix = "$", scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k")),
  ne_map("median_income", title = "intervals") +
    scale_fill_map("hcl::Batlow", type = "intervals", style = "fisher", n = 5,
                   labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                      scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k", digits = 0)) +
    bottom_legend(),
  ne_map("income_ord", title = "ordinal") +
    scale_fill_map("hcl::Batlow", type = "ordinal") + bottom_legend(1),
  ne_map("state", title = "categorical") +
    scale_fill_map("brewer::Set3", type = "categorical") + bottom_legend(2),
  ne_map("median_income", title = "rank") +
    scale_fill_map("hcl::Batlow", type = "rank",
                   labels = label_map(prefix = "$", scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k")) +
    bottom_legend(1)
)
wrap_plots(maps5, ncol = 2) & theme(legend.position = "bottom",
                                     legend.text = element_text(size = 8))
```

The **rank** type deserves a word. It colours each county by where it sits in
the distribution — the median county gets the middle colour whatever its value
— which makes it immune to outliers and skew. It is, in effect, a quantile
classification with as many classes as there are counties. Its legend keys are
placed at quantiles of the data, because a colour bar with evenly spaced
*values* would put its ticks in the wrong places.

## Two variables on one map: bivariate choropleths

### The idea, and its limits

A bivariate choropleth colours each area by two variables at once. Each
variable is classed into `n` intervals, giving `n × n` combinations, and each
combination gets one colour from an `n × n` grid. The technique dates to Judy
Olson's work at the Census Bureau in the 1970s [@olson1975]; its modern form —
a 3 × 3 grid built from two sequential hues that darken together — was set out
by Joshua Stevens and has become the standard in newsroom cartography
[@stevens2015; @leonowicz2006].

The point of a bivariate map is *relationship*: where are both variables high,
where is one high and the other low. It is a map of a correlation and its
exceptions. It is not a good way to read either variable on its own, and nine
colours is close to the limit of what a reader can match back to a legend, so
3 × 3 is the convention, 4 × 4 is readable, and more is not [@stevens2015].

### Palette

ggcarto ships two kinds of preset. *Corner* palettes are defined by four
colours — both low (near white), `x` high, `y` high, both high (dark) — and
filled in between, so they work at any `n`. *Grid* palettes are the complete
3 × 3 schemes Joshua Stevens published for bivariate maps [@stevens2015],
the ones the biscale package popularised (`"stevens-purpleblue"` and
friends), resampled when `n` is not 3. You can also pass four corner colours
of your own, a full `k × k` grid of colours, two sequential ramps to multiply
the way a printer overlays inks, or, with cols4all installed, one of its
bivariate palettes as `"c4a::<name>"`.

```{r}
#| label: bipal
bivariate_palette("blue-red", n = 3)
names(bivariate_palettes())
```

```{r}
#| label: bipal-all
#| fig-height: 6
plot_bivariate_palettes()
```

```{r}
#| label: bipal-gallery
#| fig-height: 2.6
wrap_plots(
  legend_bivariate("blue-red", 3, "x", "y", text_size = 8),
  legend_bivariate("purple-green", 3, "x", "y", text_size = 8),
  legend_bivariate(c("#f3f3f3", "steelblue", "firebrick", "#2b1b2b"), 4,
                   "x", "y", text_size = 8),
  legend_bivariate(list(x = "brewer::Blues", y = "brewer::Reds"), 3,
                   "x", "y", text_size = 8),
  nrow = 1
)
```

### Building the map: classify, colour, legend

Three steps. First, class both variables into one factor. Quantile breaks are
the usual choice because they guarantee every row and column of the legend has
counties in it — an empty row in a 3 × 3 legend is confusing. Income is
skewed, so it is classed on a log scale: `trans_x = "log10"` does that, and the
break points are still reported in dollars, so the legend needs no
back-transforming by hand.

```{r}
#| label: bi-classify
cty$bi <- classify_bivariate(cty$median_income, cty$pct_bachelors, n = 3,
                             style_x = "quantile", style_y = "quantile",
                             trans_x = "log10")
table(cty$bi)
attr(cty$bi, "breaks_x")
attr(cty$bi, "breaks_y")
```

Second, colour the map. `scale_fill_bivariate()` keeps all nine classes even if
one is empty, so map and legend always agree, and it draws no legend of its
own.

Third, the legend. A ggplot2 legend is a column of keys; a bivariate legend has
to be a grid, so `legend_bivariate()` draws it as a small ggplot and
`inset_legend()` places it on the map. Passing `classes =` hands it the break
points — already in the original units; `ends = FALSE` labels only the
interior cut points, which is cleaner.

```{r}
#| label: bi-map
#| fig-height: 6
bimap <- ggplot(cty) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = bi), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_bivariate("purple-green", n = 3) +
  labs(title = "Income and education, Northeast counties") +
  theme(legend.position = "none", plot.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"))

fmt_k <- function(x) paste0("$", round(x / 1000), "k")
leg <- legend_bivariate("purple-green", classes = cty$bi,
                        style = "diamond", ends = FALSE, text_size = 8,
                        xlab = "Median income", ylab = "% with a degree",
                        labels = function(x) ifelse(x > 1000, fmt_k(x), paste0(round(x), "%")),
                        background = alpha("white", 0.9))

inset_legend(bimap, leg, position = "topleft", width = 0.32)
```

Dark teal on this map is "high income *and* many graduates": the suburbs of
Boston, New York and Philadelphia, 52 counties. Pale grey is the opposite
corner, 55 counties of rural Pennsylvania, upstate New York and northern Maine.
The two off-diagonal corners are nearly empty — two counties are high-income
with few graduates (Salem, NJ and Adams, PA), and one is low-income with many
(Windham, VT) — and that near-emptiness *is* the finding: in this region income
and education move together, and the map is a map of the exceptions. They sit
in the in-between cells: the mid-income, high-education college counties
(Tompkins, NY, home of Cornell, is one) in light green, and the
higher-income, lower-education commuter counties in light purple. That is
exactly what a single-variable map cannot show.

`counts = TRUE` writes the number of counties in every cell of the legend, and
an empty or nearly empty cell is the first thing to look for:

```{r}
#| label: bi-counts
#| fig-height: 3
legend_bivariate("purple-green", classes = cty$bi, counts = TRUE,
                 xlab = "Income", ylab = "% degree", ends = FALSE,
                 labels = function(x) ifelse(x > 1000, fmt_k(x), paste0(round(x), "%")))
```

### Legend layouts

Two layouts. `style = "square"` has an arrowed axis on each side and reads like
a chart. `style = "diamond"` is the square rotated 45°, both-low at the bottom
and both-high at the top; values run along the two lower edges, or
`corner_labels` puts a short phrase at each corner and drops the numbers
altogether. The corner-phrase version is the most readable for a general
audience, because it says what a colour *means* rather than what the numbers
are.

```{r}
#| label: bi-legends
#| fig-height: 3
wrap_plots(
  legend_bivariate("blue-red", classes = cty$bi, xlab = "Income", ylab = "% degree",
                   ends = FALSE, text_size = 9,
                   labels = function(x) ifelse(x > 1000, fmt_k(x), paste0(round(x), "%"))),
  legend_bivariate("blue-red", 4, style = "diamond",
                   xlab = "% Black", ylab = "% Hispanic",
                   breaks_x = c(0, 5, 20, 50, 95), breaks_y = c(0, 5, 20, 50, 95),
                   labels = label_map(suffix = "%"), text_size = 9),
  legend_bivariate("blue-yellow", 3, style = "diamond", text_size = 8,
                   corner_labels = c("Low income\nfew graduates",
                                     "High income\nfew graduates",
                                     "Low income\nmany graduates",
                                     "High income\nmany graduates")),
  nrow = 1
)
```

## Project defaults

If every map in a report should use the same palettes, set them once.
`ggcarto_palettes()` sets what the package reaches for when `palette` is not
given; on ggplot2 4.0 and later, `theme_palettes()` pushes the same choices
into ggplot2's own default scales so layers you have not styled match the ones
you have.

```{r}
#| label: defaults
#| fig-height: 5
old <- ggcarto_palettes(seq = "hcl::Batlow", div = "brewer::BrBG", cat = "brewer::Dark2")
ne_map(title = "No palette argument: uses the project default") +
  scale_fill_intervals(style = "fisher", n = 5,
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", digits = 1, suffix = "%"))
ggcarto_palettes(seq = old$seq, div = old$div, cat = old$cat)   # restore
```

## How ggcarto relates to what already exists

ggplot2 and its extensions already cover a lot of this ground. ggcarto exists
for the part in between.

| Tool | What it does well | What it does not do |
|---|---|---|
| **ggplot2** `scale_fill_binned()`, `scale_fill_fermenter()`, `scale_fill_steps()` [@wickham2016] | Binned scales with a stepped colour bar | Breaks and function limits come from the *limits*, so every data-driven classification silently becomes equal intervals; no interval labels; out-of-bounds values are dropped, not squished; no midpoint anchoring for binned scales |
| **scales** | Breaks and labels for charts (`breaks_pretty()`, `label_dollar()`) | No cartographic classification, no range labels |
| **classInt** [@classint] | Every classification algorithm, the reference implementation | Only computes the numbers; you still cut the data, build a manual scale and write the legend yourself; samples above 3,000 values |
| **tmap** [@tennekes2018] | Complete thematic mapping with classification, legends, layout | Its own grammar, not ggplot2; you cannot mix it with ggplot2 layers, themes, facets or patchwork |
| **biscale** [@biscale] | Bivariate maps in ggplot2, with Stevens's palettes | Bivariate only; its own break styles and palette names |
| **RColorBrewer, viridis, cols4all, paletteer, rcartocolor, scico** | Palettes | Palettes only, each with its own syntax |
| **colorspace** [@zeileis2020] | Colour science: HCL, colour-vision simulation, palette assessment | Not about maps or scales |
| **sf, ggspatial** | Geometry, projections, scale bars, basemaps | Nothing about colour scales |
| **mapsf, cartography** | Thematic maps in base graphics | Not ggplot2 |

ggcarto is the layer that connects these inside ordinary ggplot2: it fixes the
binned-scale trap so classInt's algorithms actually work in a ggplot2 scale;
it reads palettes from every source above through one syntax; it adds the
map-shaped defaults (squish, midpoint, NA key, range labels); it makes the
mapping type a single argument, the way tmap does; it does bivariate maps with
the same break styles and palette syntax as everything else; and — the part
this version adds — it shows its working, so the classification, the class
count and the palette can each be inspected, defended and diagnosed.

What it deliberately does not do: geometry (use sf), projections and basemaps
(use sf and ggspatial), interactivity (use tmap or leaflet), or its own
palettes (use the ones that have been tested).

## Function reference, in one place

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `scale_fill_map()` / `scale_colour_map()` | The engine; `type` picks the mapping |
| `scale_fill_intervals()`, `_cont()`, `_cat()`, `_ord()`, `_rank()` | Same engine with `type` fixed |
| `class_guide()` | Suggest a number of classes, with the reasons and the metrics |
| `class_summary()` | The classes as a table: bounds, labels, counts |
| `plot_breaks()`, `compare_breaks()` | The breaks on the histogram, one method or several |
| `diagnose_map()`, `diagnose_scale()` | The decisions inside a finished scale, with warnings |
| `check_palette()`, `plot_palette()` | Lightness, distinguishability, colour-vision simulation |
| `breaks_fisher(n)`, `breaks_quantile(n)`, `breaks_sd()`, `breaks_headtails()`, ... | Break functions; usable in any ggplot2 binned scale |
| `compute_breaks(x, style, n)` | The numbers, outside ggplot2; exact and reproducible |
| `map_styles()`, `map_styles_info()` | Which styles exist and what they do |
| `as_palette()`, `map_palettes()`, `show_palette()`, `palette_sources()` | Palette access |
| `label_map()` | Legend labels: ranges, open ends, `$`, `%`, thousands |
| `trim_limits()`, `symmetric_limits()` | Data-driven limits |
| `na_key()` | A "No data" legend key for interval and continuous scales |
| `classify_bivariate()`, `scale_fill_bivariate()`, `bivariate_palette()` | Bivariate classes and colours, with per-variable styles and transforms |
| `legend_bivariate()`, `inset_legend()` | The grid legend and where to put it |
| `ggcarto_palettes()`, `theme_palettes()` | Project-wide defaults |
| `theme_ggcarto()`, `ggcarto_colours()` | The map theme used here, and its colours |
| `bivariate_palettes()`, `plot_bivariate_palettes()` | The bivariate presets, listed and drawn |
| `northeast_counties` | The data used here |

The companion article *What a good choropleth has, and how ggcarto measures
it* (`vignette("good-maps")`) goes through every metric these functions
print and the design convention behind it.

## Recipes

```{r}
#| label: recipes
#| eval: false
# The workflow
class_guide(cty$x, "fisher")                  # inspect and choose
class_summary(cty$x, "fisher", 5)             # classify
plot_breaks(cty$x, "fisher", 5)
p <- ggplot(cty) + geom_sf(aes(fill = x)) +   # map
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "fisher", 5, range = c(0.15, 1),
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", open = TRUE),
                       na.value = "grey85") +
  na_key("No data")
diagnose_map(p)                               # diagnose

# Money
scale_fill_intervals("hcl::Batlow", style = "quantile", n = 5,
                     labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                        big.mark = ",", digits = 0))

# A rate, diverging around the regional figure
scale_fill_intervals("brewer::RdBu", reverse = TRUE, n = 6, midpoint = 4.6,
                     limits = symmetric_limits(4.6),
                     labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%", digits = 1))

# Counts: integer breaks, "0 to 4" labels, a policy threshold that means it
scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", style = "quantile", n = 5, as_count = TRUE)
scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlOrRd", breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 20, 100), closure = "left",
                     labels = label_map(style = "interval", open = TRUE))

# Counts with a long tail
scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", style = "headtails",
                     labels = label_map(style = "interval", big.mark = ","))

# Same breaks on every map in a series
brks <- c(0, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10)
scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlOrRd", breaks = brks,
                     labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%", open = TRUE))

# Outlier-proof, no decisions required
scale_fill_rank("brewer::YlGnBu")

# Two variables, one of them on a log scale
cty$cls <- classify_bivariate(cty$income, cty$degree, n = 3, trans_x = "log10")
map + scale_fill_bivariate("purple-green")
inset_legend(map, legend_bivariate("purple-green", classes = cty$cls,
                                   style = "diamond", ends = FALSE,
                                   xlab = "Income", ylab = "% degree"))
```
